## Overview

Your team will choose a problem or opportunity and propose a research study
that could help a decision maker address it. Explain what you would study,
how you would collect information, and what the proposed design would allow
you to conclude.

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Scope"}
This is a study-design and research-proposal exercise. You are not carrying
out the research. Do not collect data, recruit participants, conduct a survey
or experiment, or run analyses for this project. Describe what you would do
if the proposed study were carried out.
:::

The Written Research Proposal is **one document**, about **2-4 pages in
paragraph form**. Use subheadings to organize the required components below.
The proposal outline is a planning guide for that paper, not a separate
submission. An outline or executive summary alone does not replace the paper.

## Timeline

### Week 12 - Choose Teammates and Explore Topics

Decide who you will work with and start discussing possible topics between
this week and next. Identify a problem, opportunity, or decision that your
team could develop into a research proposal.

### Week 13 - Informal Topic Meeting

Bring a proposed topic to the in-class discussion. This meeting is worth
**10 points**. Your team should be ready to explain the problem, the research
question, who or what you would study, a possible source of information, and
why the proposed method fits the question.

Use the discussion to narrow the topic and work through design choices.

### Week 14 - Pitch and Critique

Present your proposed study and participate in the critique exercise.
Use the feedback and your responses to revise the written proposal.

### Before the Final Exam - Written Research Proposal

Submit your complete proposal in the Project 2 Canvas assignment. Include
all teammates' names. The assignment uses a text-entry box, so paste the
complete paper there with its subheadings. Check Canvas for your section's
deadline.

## Choosing a Topic

You may use a business situation you know through work or personal experience,
a question connected to your major, or another topic that interests your team.
Identify who would use the results and what decision the study could inform.

You may propose a method beyond those practiced in class if you can explain
how it works and why it fits the question. Keep the design specific enough
that someone could understand how the study would be conducted.

## In-Class Topic Meeting, Pitch, and Critique

### Topic Exploration and Informal Meeting - 10 Points

Between Weeks 12 and 13, discuss possible topics with your teammates. Consider
what interests your team, who would use the results, and which question could
be addressed through a proposed study.

Bring a proposed topic to the Week 13 meeting. Explain the problem or
opportunity, a possible research question, who or what you would study, and
how you might obtain the information. Discuss why the approach fits and which
design choices still need work. Use the feedback to narrow the topic and
develop the proposal.

### Week 14 Format

Teams will work in small sets of two or three teams. One team presents while
the other team or teams critique the proposal. Rotate so every team presents
and critiques. In a three-team set, two teams critique each presentation.

### Research Proposal Pitch - 10 Points

Explain the problem, research question, proposed study design, reasons for
your design choices, and the main risks or limitations. Respond to questions
about how you would sample, measure, and collect information.

### Red Team Critique Exercise - 10 Points

Examine the other team's sampling, measures, design, conclusions, and ethical
considerations. Identify specific weaknesses and suggest changes the team
could make. Discuss your feedback with the presenting team.

The critique is part of the in-class exercise. Use the Canvas Red Team review
activity during class. Its 10 points are included in the Project 2 rubric.

## Written Research Proposal

Write **one 2-4 page paper in paragraph form** covering the following topics.
These are sections of the same paper. They are not separate assignments or
files. Describe the proposed work using language such as "we would sample"
and "the study would measure."

### 1. Problem or Opportunity

Describe the situation, why it matters, and the decision it could inform.
Identify the decision maker or other people who would use the results.

### 2. Research Question

State a focused question that your study could answer. Explain its scope
and how the answer would help with the decision. Short research objectives
or a tentative hypothesis may help clarify your question.

### 3. Proposed Study Design and Measures

Explain whether you would use a survey, observational study, experiment,
predictive model, or another approach, and why it fits your question.

Describe the population, who or what you would include, how you would select
them, what you would measure, and how you would collect the information.
Define the main concepts and explain how you would measure them.

Describe these plans without collecting data or conducting the study.

### 4. Sampling, Measurement, and Conclusions

Explain how your choices affect the evidence the study could produce.

- Who would be represented, and who might be missed?
- Could the sampling or measurement process bias the results?
- What could the study tell the decision maker?
- What generalizations or causal claims would the design support?
- For a predictive study, how would you check performance on new cases?

### 5. Risks, Limitations, and Ethics

Discuss specific ways the proposed study could go wrong and how you would
address them. Consider privacy, consent, fairness, and possible harm or
exclusion. Explain what limitations would remain and how they would affect
the conclusions.

### 6. Optional Supporting Detail

You may describe an expected pattern or briefly explain how you would analyze
the proposed data. No calculations, statistical output, charts of results,
or completed analysis are required. Keep any proposed analysis tied to the
research question and study design.

Use the [Research Proposal Outline](../week12/readings/analysis-plan-outline.qmd)
to plan the paper. The grading rubric is attached to the Project 2 assignment
in Canvas.

## Grading

The in-class work is worth 30 points. The written proposal is worth 70 points,
scored across four criteria within the same document.

Explain your design choices and their limitations clearly. A proposal that
recognizes a problem and explains how to address it is more useful than one
that overlooks it. Your grade reflects the proposed design and your reasoning,
not results from research you have carried out.
